overview: Nekoware v1's 'Reach' module is not a reach cheat: its entire body is the FastPlace pattern, a single @Handler-flagged Consumer that writes mc.rightClickDelayTimer = 0 on every UpdateEvent. The identical lambda ships unmodified as Nekoware's own FastPlace module (me/nekoWare/client/module/misc/FastPlace.java), so Reach is a mislabeled duplicate: it accelerates right-click item use and block placement by removing the vanilla 4-tick cooldown and does nothing to attack range, entity interaction, the reach attribute or the C02 attack packet. It is registered under Category.COMBAT and presents as a combat module in the module list, but the file contains no reach constant, no mixin, no packet hook and no attack code of any kind.

sections.p: The file is 22 lines. The constructor registers the module as 'Reach' under Category.COMBAT with key 0, and a single public Consumer field eventConsumer0, marked with the lwjeb @Handler marker, executes mc.rightClickDelayTimer = 0 on every UpdateEvent. There are no settings, no onEnable/onDisable, no attack hooks and no reach logic. The lambda is byte-for-byte the same statement as me/nekoWare/client/module/misc/FastPlace.java, differing only in class name, registration strings and category, which marks the module as a copy-paste artifact rather than a stubbed or half-finished feature.

Zeroing rightClickDelayTimer removes two vanilla behaviors in this fork's Minecraft.java: the 4-tick cooldown that rightClickMouse writes on every right-click action (line 1327) and the held-use gate that only fires rightClickMouse() while the timer reads exactly 0 (line 1791), with the timer otherwise decremented once per tick (lines 1453-1454). The observable effect is an accelerated right-click cadence: faster block placement and item use, up to the 20/s tick ceiling. It has zero effect on entity combat: the C02 attack path is untouched, the player's reach attribute is untouched, and hit detection still uses the vanilla 3-block entity interaction range, so attacks cannot land from beyond normal distance with this module on.

sections.h: Relationship to a real reach cheat
sections.p: A functional reach module either widens the client-side interaction ray trace (the EntityRenderer/PlayerControllerMP attack-distance check), raises the reach attribute, or otherwise lets C02 attacks target entities beyond the vanilla 3-block range. This module does none of those: the C02 packets sent by Nekoware's Aura are identical whether it is on or off, and the module cannot influence which entity an attack packet selects. The name is the only combat-relevant property it has; functionally it is a second FastPlace toggle living in the combat category.

files.label: Reach.java (module logic)
files.explanation: The complete file: the constructor (lines 11-13) registers under Category.COMBAT, and the @Handler-flagged Consumer (lines 15-18) contains only mc.rightClickDelayTimer = 0. The imports are limited to Module, UpdateEvent and Consumer; there is no reference to entities, reach, attributes or packets anywhere. Comparing it with me/nekoWare/client/module/misc/FastPlace.java shows the two files are the same module under different names and categories.

files.label: Minecraft.java (the timer gate being modified)
files.explanation: The three rightClickDelayTimer touchpoints of this fork: the field (line 244), the write of 4 at the top of rightClickMouse (line 1327), the per-tick decrement (lines 1453-1454) and the held-use branch at line 1791 that requires the timer to read exactly 0. Together they prove the module's only effect is on the right-click cadence; nothing in this file or the module connects the timer to attack distance.

countering.label: fight.Reach (lag-compensated attack trace)
countering.explanation: NCP fight.Reach measures every attack from the attacker's eye against NCP's own ray-traced entity bounds: the per-hit distance lenpRel is the eye-to-box distance minus the precision inset (line 218), and any excess over the distanceLimit accumulates into reachVL with TickTask lag adaption below 1.5f (lines 262-265), the limit deriving from the player's max attack reach (3.0 survival). A genuine interaction-range extension shows up as lenpRel above the limit on the first far hit. The Nekoware module cannot be caught by it because it never extends range and never alters the C02 the check consumes; its real fingerprint (the accelerated C08 placement stream) is invisible to this check, which is exactly the reach-family gap the mislabeled module hides in.

countering.label: EntityInteractReach (interaction distance bound)
countering.explanation: Hawk's EntityInteractReach compares the eye-to-victim-AABB distance against maxReach (3.1 survival, 5.0 creative, lines 44-45) on every entity-interact packet and flags the hit beyond it (lines 68-82). A real reach hack that lets C02 attacks land at 3.5-4 blocks trips it on the first such hit. The Nekoware module sends nothing and extends nothing, so it is invisible to the check; the 3.1 bound is what a functional reach module in this client lineage would have to defeat, and this file does not even attempt it, because it never touches entity interaction at all.

countering.label: Reach (prediction-based reach with angle pass)
countering.explanation: Grim's Reach runs on lag-compensated player state: maxReach comes from the entity interaction attribute plus a movement allowance (line 263), the minimum reach to the target box comes from ReachUtils.getMinReachToBox with the hitbox margin and a 0.0005 threshold, and an additional angle-scored pass (tickBetterReachCheckWithAngle, line 228) plus block-impossible-hits handling close the jitter gaps. Its design goal is to flag extended reach even under ping variance. The Nekoware module produces none of the attack-range deltas the check consumes, and it also delivers none of the advantage a real reach cheat grants, so enabling it changes nothing Grim can measure on the combat layer while a genuine reach module in the same client would be flagged on the first extended hit.
